newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN SANLAM TO RESHAPE FOR POST-APARTHEID ERA.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN SANLAM TO RESHAPE FOR POST-APARTHEID ERA.

text.p: Mutual life insurer Sanlam plans to scale back its industrial portfolio and may seek a listing, in a move analysts said showed local business adjusting to the post-apartheid era by untangling complex equity holdings.
Sanlam was founded in 1918 as an effective tool for extending the economic influence of the former ruling Afrikaner white minority.
But analysts on Wednesday said the planned restructuring showed it was now running itself on business lines, not ideological ones.
"It will be wonderful. Sanlam used to do things for the Afrikaner, now they are doing things for themselves," said one insurance analyst who declined to be identified.

Sanlam chairman Marinus Daling this week told the Financial Times of London that the group, South Africa's second biggest life insurer, would consider converting to a listed firm in three to four years.

Daling also said Sanlam wanted to cut its 20 billion rand portfolio holding in South Africa's industrial sector so that the group ceases to exercise control and instead develops a more normal portfolio of investments.
Sanlam, with an enormous spread of investments, has already played a leading role in forcing through some of South Africa's largest corporate break-ups.
It pushed Gencor to shed its non-mining operations and is also central to the unbundling of consumer goods firm Malbak .
Its own planned overhaul adds to a long list of corporate unbundlings as firms seek to strip away costly and inefficient layers of management and accommodate demands for black economic empowerment.
The biggest black empowerment deal so far is the National Empowerment Consortium's move to take control of Johnnies Industrial Corp .

Analysts said Sanlam's move had been widely expected. They said the firm needed to demutualise to raise cash more easily to fund its desire to become a focused financial services group with overseas ambitions.
"The main reason to demutualise is to gain access to capital," said Steven Nathan, insurance analyst at Ivor Jones.
South African foreign exchange controls severely hamper the ability of the country's firms to invest abroad, leading to a tangle of domestic cross-investments that can leave market-watchers baffled.

However, life insurers have the advantage of being able to engage in limited asset swaps with overseas investors. Analysts said Sanlam could be planning to do more of this, but that the controls, which South Africa's government has a stated aim of removing, would have to go before any major expansion occurs.
"In order to move aggressively overseas, exchange controls would have to be abolished," Nathan said.
Analysts said Sanlam's stated time scale for listing would give ample time for movement on the exchange controls problem, but was also a product of the logistical headache demutualising presents.
"It will be an enormous task to organise. They are just being sensible about the time scale," said another analyst.
With Sanlam mulling a listing, market attention may turn next to the country's biggest life insurer Old Mutual, which together with Sanlam has 65 percent of the South African market.

But analysts said the group was unlikely to follow suit as its capital position is seen as much stronger than its rivals. "Their capital positon is so strong, they don't need to do it," said one analyst.

If, or when, Sanlam goes ahead with a listing, many of its policy-holders are likely to reap a windfall bonus in a manner similar to that expected from other life insurers with demutualising aims, such as Britain's Norwich Union.
